cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Climate change is one of the greatest global challenges, caused by greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: The UK has committed to net zero carbon emissions by 2050 — the first major economy to do so. This requires transforming energy, transport, and industry. The Climate Change Committee monitors progress.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Extreme poverty has declined globally but inequality persists both between and within nations. The richest 1% own nearly half the world's wealth. Global cooperation on trade, aid, and debt relief is essential.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set 17 targets for a better world by 2030, including: no poverty, zero hunger, quality education, gender equality, clean water, climate action, and reduced inequalities.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Global health crises like COVID-19 demonstrate the need for international cooperation — viruses do not respect borders, and vaccine distribution requires global coordination.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Conflicts and refugees are global issues: over 100 million people are forcibly displaced worldwide. The UNHCR coordinates refugee protection, but host countries bear most responsibility.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Sustainable development balances three pillars: economic growth, social inclusion, and environmental protection. Progress in one area should not come at the expense of the others.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Individual actions (recycling, reducing energy use, choosing sustainable products) contribute to sustainability, but systemic change through government policy and corporate responsibility is also essential.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Fair trade ensures producers in developing countries receive fair prices, decent working conditions, and sustainable farming practices. Look for the Fairtrade Mark on products.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Water scarcity, deforestation, and biodiversity loss are interconnected environmental challenges that require coordinated international action.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: Global citizenship means taking responsibility for the impact of our choices on others worldwide — recognising that our consumption, travel, and political choices affect people in other countries.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Global Issues & Sustainability
cards.back: The UK has a key role in addressing global issues through its aid budget, diplomatic influence, military capability, and leadership in international organisations.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — global issues & sustainability?
cards.back: 1. For Global Issues & Sustainability questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Global Issues & Sustainability to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate the view that global citizenship requires individuals to take action on climate change. [12 marks]

AO2 (Analysis & Evaluation — 40%): You must analyse and evaluate different viewpoints, policies, and approaches related to global issues & sustainability.
